summary: This RFC describes a method adopted by CSNET, the VAN gateway, and other organizations for carrying IP datagrams across X.25-based public data networks. It was later replaced by RFC 1356.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 877 specifies how to carry IP datagrams over X.25 public data networks by identifying IP in the call and sending each datagram as a complete packet sequence. RFC 1356 later replaced this standard.

questions: how to send ip datagrams over x.25
how to send ip over x.25
how does rfc 877 carry ip over x.25
what identifies ip in an x.25 call
subtitle: A method for sending IP datagrams over X.25 public data networks

tldr.problem: X.25 public data networks use virtual circuits, while IP sends datagrams, so the two need a defined way to carry datagrams between them.
tldr.mechanism: The call identifies IP with the value CC in its first Call User Data octet, and X.25 packets carry each IP datagram as a complete packet sequence.
tldr.outcome: RFC 877 was later replaced by RFC 1356.

facts.label: IP identifier in Call User Data

sections.title: Opening an X.25 Virtual Circuit
sections.content:
This standard describes transmitting IP datagrams over X.25-based public data networks. A virtual circuit is opened on demand when a datagram arrives for transmission.

A virtual circuit is closed after a period of inactivity that depends on the cost of keeping it open, or if the interface runs out of virtual circuits. Either site may close a circuit; if it closes or resets while a datagram is being transmitted, that datagram is lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending interface opens an X.25 circuit when it has a datagram to send. If the circuit closes during transmission, that datagram is lost.

sections.title: Identifying and Sending IP Datagrams
sections.content:
The first octet in the Call User Data field of an X.25 Call Request identifies the protocol. The value hexadecimal CC, decimal 204, means Internet Protocol.

Each datagram is sent as an X.25 complete packet sequence and starts on a packet boundary. If it takes more than one packet, the M bit indicates that more data follows. The RFC adds no other headers or data to the packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The call begins with a value that identifies the data as IP. A datagram starts at a packet boundary, and the M bit marks packets that have more of it to follow.

sections.title: Packet Sizes and Other X.25 Features
sections.content:
Unless the sites negotiate a larger packet size, an IP datagram sent over X.25 may be at most 576 octets. The RFC gives 1024 octets as an example of a larger size that two sites may negotiate.

Features not discussed in the RFC are not used; examples include interrupt packets and the D bit. Negotiable X.25 facilities, including larger packet and window sizes, are allowed. Protocols above IP do not cause this standard to open a corresponding X.25 circuit for each connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The default maximum datagram size is 576 octets, but both sites may negotiate a larger packet size. The document leaves unmentioned X.25 features unused.

references.text: Comer, D.E. and Korb, J.T., "CSNET Protocol Software: The IP-to-X.25 Interface," SIGCOMM Symposium on Communications Architectures and Protocols, March 1983.
